description: Fixed and variable costs, revenue and how to calculate profit or loss.
content_html:
Types of Cost

Every start-up spends money before it makes money. Understanding where that money goes — and whether each cost moves with output or stays fixed — is one of the most practical skills an entrepreneur needs. Costs split into two categories: fixed costs and variable costs.

Fixed costs do not change with output. Even if a business produces nothing this week, it still has to pay them. Fixed costs for a start-up typically include:

  • Rent — the cost of business premises, whether a market stall, workshop or small office.
  • Insurance — cover for the business, its stock and public liability.
  • Advertising — a regular advert in a local newspaper or an annual subscription to a directory listing.
  • Salaries — the fixed monthly pay of permanent staff. Salaries are a fixed cost because they do not change based on how much the business produces.
  • Utilities — gas, electricity and water bills. Although bills fluctuate slightly, utilities are classified as a fixed cost for this qualification.
  • Loan interest — when a business borrows money, the interest charged on that loan is a fixed cost. Note: the loan repayment itself (paying back what was borrowed) is not classified as a business cost — it is a financial outflow, but only the interest element counts as a cost.
Key Fact

Salaries and utilities are fixed costs — they do not change with output. Wages (paid by the hour or by units produced) are a variable cost. Loan repayments are NOT a business cost; only the loan interest is a cost. These distinctions are frequently tested.

Variable Costs

Variable costs rise as output rises and fall as output falls. A baker who makes twice as many loaves uses twice as much flour — that is a variable cost in action. Common variable costs for a start-up include:

  • Raw materials — the ingredients, fabric, timber or other inputs used directly in production.
  • Packaging — boxes, bags or labels that go with each unit sold.
  • Wages — pay calculated by the hour or by the unit, so the business pays more when it produces more and less when production slows.

Total Costs

Once you know the fixed and variable costs separately, you can combine them:
Total costs = Total fixed costs + Total variable costs
This is the full amount a business spends in a given period. Knowing total costs is essential for pricing decisions, for planning whether the business will break even, and for calculating profit or loss.

Many students classify all staff pay as a variable cost. This is wrong in this qualification. Salaries are fixed monthly amounts agreed in a permanent contract — the business pays them regardless of how much is produced. Wages are tied to hours worked or units produced, so they go up and down with output. If a question names “salaries”, treat them as fixed. If it names “wages”, treat them as variable.

Revenue

Revenue is the income a business receives from selling its output. The formula is simple:
Revenue = Selling price per unit × Quantity sold

For example, if a small textile business sells tea towels at £8 each and sells 350 in a month, its revenue is £8 × 350 = £2,800. Revenue tells you how much money has come in, but not how much the business has kept — for that, you need to deduct costs.

The formula also works in reverse. If you know the revenue and the quantity sold, you can rearrange to find the selling price:
Selling price = Revenue ÷ Quantity sold

Profit and Loss

Profit is what a business keeps after paying all its costs:
Profit = Revenue − Total costs

If total costs are higher than revenue, the result is a loss — a negative figure. This is common for start-ups in their first months, when costs are high and customers are still building awareness of the business. Identifying a loss early helps the entrepreneur decide whether to adjust prices, cut costs, or both.

Key Fact

Revenue = Price × Quantity sold. Total costs = Fixed costs + Variable costs. Profit = Revenue − Total costs. These three formulas build on each other — a calculation question may ask for any one of them, or require you to rearrange to find a missing value.

Worked Example

Thornwick Brew Co is a sole trader who produces craft lemonade in Sheffield. Each bottle sells at £3.50. In June, she sold 900 bottles. Her monthly fixed costs are £780 (rent £500, insurance £130, loan interest £150). Her variable costs are £1.20 per bottle (ingredients and labels).

Revenue: £3.50 × 900 = £3,150
Total variable costs: £1.20 × 900 = £1,080
Total costs: £780 + £1,080 = £1,860
Profit: £3,150 − £1,860 = £1,290

Calculation questions do not always give you cost, price and quantity in tidy form. You may be given the revenue and the number of units and asked to find the selling price. You may be given the profit and told to work backwards to find variable cost per unit. Practise these rearrangements:

  • Find selling price: Selling price = Revenue ÷ Quantity sold
  • Find quantity sold: Quantity sold = Revenue ÷ Selling price
  • Find variable cost per unit: Variable cost per unit = Total variable costs ÷ Quantity produced

Watch for questions that give figures per year when you need to calculate per month (or vice versa). Divide annual fixed costs by 12 to get the monthly figure before substituting into the formula.
exam_tip_html: On “Calculate” questions, always write the formula before substituting numbers — the formula itself can earn a method mark even if your arithmetic goes wrong. The most common error on this topic is treating salaries as variable or treating loan repayments as a cost: if the question includes salary figures, put them under fixed costs; if it mentions a loan repayment, ignore it as a cost (only the interest counts). For 3-mark calculations, show every step clearly: find variable cost totals, then total costs, then profit. Check your units — if you start with monthly figures and the question asks for annual profit, multiply at the end. The “explain” command word means you must use because, therefore or this means that to link your point — a bare statement earns fewer marks than a developed reason chain.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Fixed costs (rent, insurance, advertising, salaries, utilities, loan interest) stay the same regardless of output. Variable costs (raw materials, packaging, wages) rise and fall with production. Only loan interest is a cost — loan repayments are not.
  • Revenue = Selling price × Quantity sold. Total costs = Fixed costs + Variable costs. Profit = Revenue − Total costs. A negative result is a loss.
  • These formulas can be rearranged. If a question gives you revenue and quantity, you can find the selling price; if it gives revenue and selling price, you can find quantity sold. Read the question carefully to see which value is missing.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is a fixed cost for a small start-up?
A) Raw materials used in production
B) Packaging for each unit sold
C) Wages paid to part-time hourly workers
D) Rent paid on workshop premises
practice_questions.marks: D) Rent paid on workshop premises [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State whether each of the following is a fixed cost or a variable cost: (i) salaries paid to full-time staff; (ii) wages paid to part-time workers by the hour.
practice_questions.marks:
(i) Fixed cost — salaries are a set monthly amount that does not change with output. [1 mark]
(ii) Variable cost — wages vary with the number of hours worked, which rises and falls with production. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
Coppice Candle Co makes artisan soy candles in Bath. In November it sold 400 candles at £9.50 each. Fixed costs for the month were £1,100 (rent £700, insurance £200, loan interest £200). Variable costs were £2.80 per candle.

Calculate the profit or loss made by Coppice Candle Co in November. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Revenue: £9.50 × 400 = £3,800
Total variable costs: £2.80 × 400 = £1,120
Total costs: £1,100 + £1,120 = £2,220
Profit: £3,800 − £2,220 = £1,580
[3 marks: 1 mark for correct revenue (£3,800); 1 mark for correct total costs (£2,220); 1 mark for correct profit figure (£1,580). Allow follow-through on arithmetic errors if method is correct.]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a business owner might be surprised to find that the business is making a loss even though monthly revenue has increased.
practice_questions.marks: A business can make a loss even as revenue rises if total costs have grown faster than revenue. For example, if the owner has taken on new fixed costs such as renting larger premises or hiring additional permanent staff on salaries, these additional fixed costs will increase total costs regardless of output level. This means that even with higher revenue coming in, the gap between revenue and total costs may widen in the wrong direction, pushing the business into loss. [1 mark for identifying that costs may have risen; 1 mark for identifying a specific cost type or example; 1 mark for a developed chain explaining the revenue–cost relationship and how this leads to a loss.]

practice_questions.text:
Ironwild Pottery is a small partnership in Derby making hand-thrown bowls. Fixed costs are £1,400 per month. Variable costs are £4.50 per bowl. In May, the business received total revenue of £5,200 from sales of 400 bowls.

Analyse whether Ironwild Pottery's current cost and revenue structure gives it a healthy financial position.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Accurate calculation of profit (revenue £5,200; variable costs £1,800; total costs £3,200; profit £2,000) with well-developed analysis of what that profit means for the partnership's financial health. Considers the implications of fixed vs variable costs — for example, if sales fall, the fixed costs remain, quickly eroding or eliminating profit. Reaches a supported conclusion about the risks and strengths of the current structure.

Secure (3–4 marks): Correct or near-correct calculation with some analytical comment on the cost structure or profit margin. Applies to Ironwild's context but may not fully develop the implications of fixed costs remaining constant if output falls.

Developing (2 marks): Calculates revenue or costs but does not reach a profit figure, or identifies the cost classification without analysis.

Emerging (1 mark): States a relevant term or makes a basic arithmetic attempt with no developed analysis.

practice_questions.text:
Glassroot Jewellery is a sole trader in Bristol selling handmade silver earrings. The owner, Priya, borrowed £8,000 to buy equipment. She repays £350 per month, of which £80 is interest and £270 is repayment of the loan itself. She also pays £600 per month in salaries to one part-time assistant on a fixed contract, and pays hourly wages of £9.50 to two casual workers who each work an average of 20 hours per month.

Identify which of Priya's financial outgoings are business costs and calculate her total monthly fixed and variable costs from these figures.
practice_questions.marks:
Business costs identified correctly:
• Loan interest (£80) — this IS a cost [1 mark]
• Loan repayment (£270) — this is NOT a cost; it is a repayment of borrowed capital [1 mark for correctly excluding it]
• Salary (£600) — fixed cost [1 mark]
• Casual wages: 2 workers × 20 hours × £9.50 = £380 — variable cost [1 mark]

Total monthly fixed costs = £80 (interest) + £600 (salary) = £680
Total monthly variable costs = £380 (wages)
[Full marks for correctly excluding loan repayments, correctly classifying all three costs, and showing the wage calculation. Allow follow-through on arithmetic errors if classification method is correct.]

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is classified as a fixed cost?
A start-up borrows £10,000 and makes monthly repayments of £250, of which £60 is interest. Which figure counts as a business cost?
Salaries paid to full-time permanent staff are classified as a _____ cost.
Match each item to its cost category:
right: Fixed cost — stays the same regardless of output
Variable cost — tied to hours worked or units produced
Variable cost — rises with the number of units made

flashcard_questions.a: Costs that stay the same regardless of how many units are produced or sold.

flashcard_questions.q: Are salaries a fixed or variable cost?
flashcard_questions.a: Fixed — they are set monthly amounts that do not change with output.

flashcard_questions.q: Are wages a fixed or variable cost?
flashcard_questions.a: Variable — they change with hours worked or units produced.

flashcard_questions.q: Are utility bills a fixed or variable cost in this qualification?
flashcard_questions.a: Fixed — classified as fixed even though they fluctuate slightly.

flashcard_questions.q: Which part of a loan counts as a business cost — the repayment or the interest?
flashcard_questions.a: Only the interest — loan repayments are not a business cost.

flashcard_questions.q: Formula cloze: Total costs = Total fixed costs + _____.
What does it mean if Profit = Revenue − Total costs gives a negative number?
flashcard_questions.a: The business is making a loss — costs exceed revenue.

flashcard_questions.q: Give three examples of variable costs for a small manufacturer.
flashcard_questions.a: Raw materials, packaging, and wages (any two sufficient).

flashcard_questions.q: How do you find selling price if you know revenue and quantity sold?
Why might a business need to divide annual fixed costs by 12 in a calculation question?
flashcard_questions.a: To convert them to a monthly figure when the question asks for monthly profit or costs.

glossary_terms.definition: Costs that stay the same regardless of how many units a business produces or sells, such as rent, insurance and salaries.
Costs that rise and fall directly in line with the number of units produced or sold, such as raw materials, packaging and wages.
The total money received by a business from selling its products or services; calculated as selling price multiplied by quantity sold.
The amount left over after total costs are deducted from total revenue; a negative figure means the business is making a loss.
